h1: Hazy pale ale or hazy IPA? Where the line between them sits
title: Hazy Pale Ale vs Hazy IPA | Craft Beer School
desc: Hazy pale ale and hazy IPA look alike in the glass. Here is how strength, hop dose, body and bitterness separate them and how to tell by taste.
teaser: Same cloudy glass, same tropical smell. So why does one cost more and hit harder?
standfirst: Put a hazy pale ale next to a hazy IPA and you may struggle to tell them apart by eye. The line between them is real, though. It runs through strength, hop load and body. Once you know where to look you can taste it.
sections: Two beers from the same family

Both beers come out of the same movement: the soft, juicy, cloudy style that grew up in New England in the 2010s and spread everywhere, including Indian taprooms. Brewers use a grist with plenty of oats or wheat, a yeast that leaves fruity esters, light bitterness and a heavy dose of aroma hops added late in the boil and during fermentation. Our New England IPA guide explains the full method.

The pale ale and the IPA versions use that same toolkit. What changes is how hard each tool is pushed.

The clearest difference is alcohol. A hazy pale ale usually sits around 4.5 to 5.5% ABV. A hazy IPA typically lands somewhere between 6 and 7.5%. A double or imperial version goes higher. More malt means more alcohol, more body and more sweetness to balance against the hops.

The Brewers Association, which runs the largest American competitions, lists juicy or hazy pale ale and juicy or hazy IPA as separate categories, largely along these strength lines. Guidelines are a reference rather than a law. A brewer in Bengaluru can call a 5.8% beer whatever they like. Treat the label as a hint, then check the ABV on the menu.
Hop dose and what it does to aroma

An IPA carries more hops, mostly as dry hops added during and after fermentation. That shows up as a louder, more layered aroma: mango, passion fruit, citrus pith, sometimes a green or dank edge. A hazy pale ale is lighter on the dry hop, so the aroma is brighter but simpler. The malt and yeast have more room to speak.

Heavy dry hopping has a side effect that you can feel. Hop particles and polyphenols add a slight grip or burn at the back of the throat, sometimes called hop burn. In a big hazy IPA that is common. In a well-made hazy pale ale it should be almost absent.

The hop choice tends to be similar across both. Citra, Mosaic, Galaxy and Nelson Sauvin turn up again and again because they carry the tropical fruit character drinkers expect. The pale ale simply uses less of them, sometimes with one variety where the IPA uses three.

Neither style is meant to be very bitter. Brewers move most of their hop additions late precisely so they get aroma without harsh bitterness. Even so, a hazy IPA has more of everything, so the finish tends to be fuller and slightly sweeter, with a lingering fruity bitterness. A hazy pale ale should finish cleaner and drier, the kind of beer you can drink two of without feeling weighed down.

Here is a practical test. Take a sip, swallow and wait ten seconds. If the flavour fades quickly and you want another sip, you are probably in pale ale territory. If it coats the mouth and keeps going, that is the IPA.
Why freshness matters even more for both

Hazy beers are among the least stable on the shelf. The haze proteins drop out, hop aroma fades and oxygen turns that bright fruit into something flat and sweetish. In Indian conditions, where a can may spend hours in a warm van, the cold chain decides whether you taste the beer the brewer made. Always check the canning date, buy from a fridge and drink it within weeks rather than months. Our guide to fresh and stale IPA shows what the change tastes like.
How to taste the difference yourself

The best way to learn the line is to taste the two side by side. Pour a small measure of each into identical glasses at the same temperature, around 7 to 10 °C. Smell both before tasting. Note the intensity of the aroma, then the weight of the beer on your tongue, then the finish. Write one line for each. After three or four of these comparisons you will start guessing the style before you read the menu.

That is the gap most drinkers never close. They can say they like a beer, but not why, or how it differs from the one next to it. Training your palate to separate strength, hop intensity and body is a skill. It gets faster with structure.
faqs: Is a hazy IPA always stronger than a hazy pale ale?
Usually. Hazy pale ales tend to be around 4.5 to 5.5% ABV and hazy IPAs around 6 to 7.5%, but brewers do not all follow the same lines, so check the stated ABV.
Oats and wheat in the grist, a yeast that stays in suspension and proteins bound to hop compounds all keep the beer hazy. The haze is intended, not a sign of a fault.
Start with the hazy pale ale. It shows the soft, juicy character of the style at a lighter strength, which makes it easier to taste what the hops are doing.
